title: AFP tech investment and overdue HKMA STR findings demand action now
summary: Three AFP enforcement items converge on a single operational question: are your transaction monitoring controls calibrated for digital payments and online harm typologies? Plus, the HKMA's overdue STR quality thematic review is still open for roughly a quarter of supervised institutions. Alex and Jordan disagree on where to focus first.
script:
ALEX: Let me put a specific question on the table to open today. The Australian Federal Police have now, in the space of a single week, charged a man over identity-based public sector fraud, charged a second man over child sexual exploitation material, and committed fresh investment in technology to detect online harm. Three separate actions. But when I look at them together, I think they are pointing at one specific vulnerability in financial crime controls, which is whether transaction monitoring systems are actually calibrated for digital payment flows connected to online exploitation. Jordan, is that a fair read, or am I forcing a pattern?

JORDAN: It's a fair read, but I want to complicate it slightly. The identity fraud case and the child exploitation case are not the same operational problem for an MLRO, even if they share a digital payments thread. The Queensland impersonation case is about procurement fraud and benefits systems, so the relevant control there is customer due diligence and beneficial ownership verification on accounts receiving government disbursements. The Sydney child exploitation case is a different typology entirely. It sits squarely in the intersection between online platforms, digital wallets, and what FATF Recommendation 40 calls the detection of proceeds of predicate offences. Those require different monitoring rules.

ALEX: Right, and I accept that distinction. Where I push back slightly is on the AFP's technology investment announcement. The agency has explicitly acknowledged that adolescents are shifting toward artificial intelligence tools in ways that create new exploitation vectors. That is a forward-looking threat statement from a law enforcement agency, and in my experience, when the AFP signals a threat shift publicly, AUSTRAC's supervisory expectations follow within a reporting cycle or two.

JORDAN: That I agree with entirely. And the practical read for Australian reporting entities under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act, specifically the Section 84 annual program review obligation, which for most institutions was due by the end of August this year, is that if your Part A risk assessment does not yet reference online exploitation typologies and emerging AI-facilitated harm, it should. If your annual review has already been filed without that coverage, you need to think about whether a mid-cycle addendum to your risk assessment is warranted before AUSTRAC comes knocking.

ALEX: So the action for Australian MLROs is explicit. Before your next quarterly transaction monitoring tuning review, look at your rule set for digital payment flows with characteristics consistent with child exploitation typologies. The AFP's investment in detection technology is a signal that referrals to AUSTRAC are going to increase, and you want your systems to surface the same patterns law enforcement is starting to surface more efficiently.

JORDAN: Exactly. And if your institution processes payments to offshore digital platforms or content services, I would not wait for the next scheduled review. Pull your monitoring team together this week.

ALEX: Moving on, and this is where I want to spend more time, because I think it is the most immediately consequential item in today's digest. The HKMA's thematic review of Suspicious Transaction Report narrative quality from the fourth quarter of last year is still open. Deficiency letters went to roughly twenty-five percent of authorised institutions earlier in 2026. If you received one of those letters, the closure of your findings is overdue. That is a high-priority obligation sitting in the digest, and my read is that some institutions are underestimating the reputational exposure of leaving this open.

JORDAN: I think you are being too generous to those institutions by calling it underestimation. Some of them know perfectly well the findings are open and are hoping the HKMA will move on to the next thematic cycle before chasing closure. That is not a strategy. The HKMA is explicit in its AML and CFT Guideline, specifically paragraph 11, about the requirement for annual self-assessment and ongoing responsiveness to supervisory findings. Letting a deficiency letter sit is not a neutral act. It is evidence in the next examination that governance and escalation are not functioning.

ALEX: That is a fair challenge. I suppose I read it as underestimation because the STR narrative quality issue is genuinely difficult to remediate fast. Writing a good SAR narrative, covering the five elements of who, what, when, where, and why in a way that is useful to the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit, requires either quality assurance capacity that many smaller authorised institutions do not have, or a significant training investment.

JORDAN: True. But that is exactly why the HKMA flagged it thematically rather than institution by institution in silence. The regulator is telling the whole sector: this is a systemic gap, and we expect you to fix it. The institutions that received deficiency letters have a higher bar. They need to show a closed-loop response, not just a training plan that runs into next quarter.

ALEX: So what should listeners in Hong Kong do?

JORDAN: Three things. First, if you received a deficiency letter, do not wait for the HKMA to follow up. Prepare your closure response now and have it reviewed by your head of financial crime before submitting. Second, even if you did not receive a letter, run a sample of your last ninety days of STR filings through a narrative quality check this month, because the self-assessment return under paragraph 11 of the HKMA guideline covers STR filing quality and you want that to be defensible. Third, for anyone whose Q3 2026 self-assessment has not yet been submitted, the September 30 deadline has passed. If you are overdue on that return, escalate to your board risk committee immediately and submit with a covering note explaining the delay. Silence to the HKMA is worse than a late filing with context.

ALEX: And on the Financial Stability Board peer review into public sector backstop funding, which dropped this week covering gaps in Key Attribute 6 of the Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes, the direct AML read-across is fairly narrow for most listeners today. The gaps identified are primarily at the sovereign fiscal architecture level rather than firm-level financial crime controls. But if you work at a systemically important financial institution where resolution planning is on your board's agenda, it is worth flagging to your prudential colleagues that the FSB peer review will likely sharpen supervisory focus on resolution-linked governance disclosures, and your MLRO function may be asked to contribute to those disclosures. Keep an eye on the FSB's published follow-up timeline.

JORDAN: Agreed. That one is a slow burn, not a Monday morning crisis.

ALEX: Before we close, the one thing to do before end of week: if you are an MLRO at an institution that received an HKMA STR quality deficiency letter, have your closure response drafted and in your line manager's inbox before Friday. The window to close this on your terms is narrowing.

JORDAN: And if that felt uncomfortably close to home, that is the point. Full source links and the obligation register are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. See you tomorrow.
